title: Morpho's ten-day timelock only protects Spark if it can exit inside the window, and the exit leg is exactly what is left unspecified
content:
Morpho USDS publishes inflow "`maxAmount`: 200,000,000 USDS, `slope`: 100,000,000 USDS per day" and outflow limits where both parameters read "This parameter will be specified in a future iteration of the Spark Artifact" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.8.2.2.4.1/.2). Morpho USDC repeats the shape with a 50,000,000 USDC inflow (.8.3.2.4.1/.2). Both instances also document a 240-hour timelock on curator action.

Put together, the two facts pull against each other. The timelock's protective value is entirely a function of what Spark can do during the delay — it grants time, and time is only worth what can be withdrawn in it. The document that specifies the delay declines to specify the withdrawal capacity.

The contrast within the same protocol family sharpens it. The Spark Blue Chip USDT Vault, also Morpho, also 240-hour timelock, publishes "`maxAmount`: unlimited, `slope`: unlimited" on the outflow leg (.8.4.2.4.2) — the configuration that makes the timelock argument work. Two vaults with identical governance exposure are documented with opposite exit guarantees, and only one of them can be verified.

This is the concrete cost of the Artifact's deferral convention. An unspecified parameter is not neutral when another parameter's safety argument depends on it: here the mitigation is documented, the mechanism the mitigation relies on is not, and nothing in the structure flags that the two are coupled.
description: Morpho USDS and USDC document inflow limits of 200,000,000 and 50,000,000 but defer both outflow parameters, so the reaction window the timelock buys has no documented capacity to use it.
